cards.title: Introduction to Sessions
cards.content:
HTTP is a stateless protocol, meaning each request from a browser is independent. Sessions allow you to store information specific to a user across multiple requests.

In Flask, sessions are implemented on top of signed cookies, meaning the user can view the content of the session, but cannot modify it without knowing the secret key.

cards.title: Importing the Session Object
cards.content:
To use sessions in Flask, you need to import the session object from the flask module.

from flask import Flask, session

app = Flask(__name__)
app.secret_key = 'your_super_secret_key'

Note: A secret_key is strictly required to securely sign the session cookie.

content.question: Why is a `secret_key` required when using Flask sessions?

options.text: To securely sign the session cookie and prevent tampering
To connect to the Flask development server

cards.title: Reading and Writing Sessions
cards.content:
Flask's session acts like a standard Python dictionary. You can assign values to keys and read them back later.

@app.route('/login')
def login():
    session['username'] = 'john_doe'
    return "Logged in!"

@app.route('/profile')
def profile():
    if 'username' in session:
        return f"Hello, {session['username']}!"
    return "You are not logged in."

content.text: To store a user's role in the Flask session dictionary, you write: session[___] = 'admin'

cards.title: Removing Data and Logging Out
cards.content:
To remove a specific key from the session, use the pop() method. To clear the entire session completely, use the clear() method.

@app.route('/logout')
def logout():
    # Remove username if it exists
    session.pop('username', None)
    # Or clear everything:
    # session.clear()
    return "Logged out!"

cards.title: Session Security Best Practices
cards.content:
Because Flask stores session data in client-side cookies, keep these security guidelines in mind:

  • Never store sensitive data like raw passwords or credit card numbers in the session.
  • Keep your secret_key complex and secret (use environment variables).
  • Flask sessions have a default lifetime (non-permanent cookies expire when the browser closes, unless session.permanent = True is set).

content.question: Where does Flask store the actual session data by default?

options.text: In the server's local file system cache

cards.title: Summary
cards.content:
Congratulations! You have learned how sessions work in Flask.

Key takeaways:

  • Always define app.secret_key.
  • Treat the session object like a Python dictionary.
  • Use session.pop() or session.clear() to log users out.
  • Never store sensitive credentials directly in session cookies.
